explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The verse says Joshua gave Caleb his portion "According to the LORD’s command to him…" So Joshua isn't making this up as he goes. He's handing out the land the way he was told, kind of like me following a recipe card instead of guessing at the flour (Joshua 15:13).

Nope, no ballots in this verse, friend. No clipboards, no show of hands. The text says Joshua gave Caleb his portion "According to the LORD’s command to him…" The command is what Joshua goes by (Joshua 15:13).

I get why you'd think so, since Hebron lands among the sons of Judah. But the verse never mentions a deal or any bargaining. It says Joshua gave Caleb a portion "According to the LORD’s command to him…" That command is the whole answer (Joshua 15:13).

You got it, baker. The verse says Caleb "…drove out from there the three sons of Anak…" the descendants of Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. Three of them, and Caleb drove them out. I can't even drive the crumbs off my counter, and they're not even big (Joshua 15:14).

Tribute? Friend, I don't see any payment plan in this verse. The text says Caleb "…drove out from there the three sons of Anak…" and that's all it says about it. No deal is mentioned, just the three sons of Anak being driven out. I once hid in a drawer for years and never once paid rent, so I'm no expert on tribute (Joshua 15:14).

A treaty? Ooh, that's a very polite guess, baker. Very civilized. Pens out, clean desk, everybody shaking hands. But there's no treaty in this verse. It says Caleb "…drove out from there the three sons of Anak…" and they're the descendants of Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. Nothing gets signed, they get driven out (Joshua 15:14).

Right on, friend. Caleb says, "To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage." That's a big promise to put on the table. I think a man who says that out loud means to keep it (Joshua 15:16).
Close on the family feel, but no. Caleb doesn't offer a servant. He says, "…I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage." The prize is his daughter, and her name is Acsah (Joshua 15:16).

Not a sister, baker. Caleb talks about his own child here. He says, "…I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage." to whoever captures Kiriath-sepher. Good guess on the family angle, though (Joshua 15:16).
Not quite, friend. Caleb doesn't back out at all. After Othniel captures the city, the verse says "…Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage." A promise made, a promise kept (Joshua 15:17).

Yes, it's false, baker. The text says Othniel captured the city, and then "…Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage." No backing out, no excuses, no "let me think about it." Caleb did just what he said he would (Joshua 15:17).

That's it, friend. When Acsah gets off her donkey, Caleb asks her, "What do you desire?" Short and kind, and it opens the door for her to ask. I'd say that's a dad who wants to hear her out (Joshua 15:18).

Good thinking, since Othniel is part of the story. But the verse has Caleb asking something else. When she gets off her donkey, he says, "What do you desire?" His question is about what she wants (Joshua 15:18).

How long she'll stay? Ha, you've got Caleb checking the calendar like a host who wants to know when the guests are leaving. Not this dad, baker. When Acsah gets off her donkey, he asks, "What do you desire?" He's asking what she wants, and I think that's a dad leaning in to listen (Joshua 15:18).

True, baker! Acsah asks for springs of water, and Caleb doesn't hold back. The verse says "So Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs." She asked, and she got the upper and the lower. I think that's a dad who loves saying yes (Joshua 15:19).
Oh, this one's a yes, friend. Caleb doesn't turn her down or hand over just half. The text says, "So Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs." Both of them, upper and lower (Joshua 15:19).

Correct, baker. The text says "…the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem." It's a little hard to read after all those cities, but it's honest. The verse says that to this day the Jebusites live there among the descendants of Judah (Joshua 15:63).

That would be a tidy ending, friend, but it's not in the text. The verse says Judah "…could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem." It also says the Jebusites live there among the descendants of Judah, so they stay (Joshua 15:63).

Nope, it goes the other way. The text says the descendants of Judah "…could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem." So the Jebusites are still there. Judah didn't finish that job (Joshua 15:63).

True, baker. The verse says, "…to this day the Jebusites live there among the descendants of Judah." So at the time of writing, they were still in Jerusalem. The list ends on that note, plain and honest (Joshua 15:63).

Not false, friend. The text says, "So to this day the Jebusites live there among the descendants of Judah." At the time this was written, they were still living in Jerusalem. The story doesn't pretend otherwise (Joshua 15:63).
